issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in this profile. With assault trauma, the other trigger items (related sounds, being naked) plausibly cue danger/vulnerability, and the threat items are about danger and vigilance. Praise/positive attention points in a very different interpersonal direction and is not supported by corresponding appraisals or threat content, so it weakens cross-node coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
issues.explanation: 'Fear going crazy' is poorly aligned with the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize external danger and vigilance, and the trigger pattern centers on assault-related cues. A dominant appraisal of losing one's mind would usually be accompanied by threat content about internal loss of control or dissociation-like danger, which is absent here.

For an assault trauma, the trigger pattern strongly suggests a sexual assault context (being naked, being looked at sexually). That is not impossible, but the rest of the profile does not support that specific context strongly enough to make the set cohere: there are no matching sexual-assault-linked threat or memory items, and the only bodily appraisal is about the body being unreliable rather than violated or contaminated.

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'I can no longer trust my own body' is more typically linked to injury, dissociation, panic-like bodily cues, or medical trauma. It does not fit well with the mainly sexual-vulnerability trigger pattern unless there is additional supporting content, which is absent here.

vignette:
Minh Tran is a 71-year-old Vietnamese American attorney, married for over four decades, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 71 following a violent assault that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. She had spent the evening at a downtown parking garage after a late client meeting, and as she walked toward her car, a man approached her from behind, grabbed her by the shoulders, and forced her against a concrete pillar. He made explicitly sexual comments while pressing against her, and when she tried to call out, he struck her across the face. The assault was interrupted only when another driver's headlights swept through the garage and the man fled. Minh was left on the ground, her heart hammering so violently she believed, in those first moments, that she was dying.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not settle into the past the way she had expected it to. Certain things kept pulling her back into the garage with a force she could neither predict nor control. The sound of footsteps on hard flooring - common enough in the marble corridors of the courthouse where she practices - could stop her mid-sentence. A door slamming somewhere down the hall, the scrape of a chair across tile: any of these could arrive without warning and return her, briefly but completely, to the sound of her own breathing against that pillar. She found herself pausing in hallways, listening, before she could continue walking. When a male colleague held her gaze a moment too long across a conference table, or when she caught a client looking at her in a way she could not immediately categorize as professional, something cold moved through her chest and she had to press her fingernails into her palm to remain in the room.

What frightened her most, perhaps, was what her own body had begun to do. If she climbed a flight of stairs too quickly, or drank coffee in the morning and felt her pulse quicken, she would go rigid with the certainty that something was about to happen - that the racing of her heart was a warning, not a physical artifact. She had come to believe that her body was no longer a reliable instrument, that it had failed to protect her once and could not be trusted to signal the difference between ordinary exertion and genuine danger. This conviction had extended outward into the world itself. She was certain, in a way she had not been before, that the world was a dangerous place and that she had simply been naive not to have seen it sooner.

By the time she sought help, a number of things in her daily life had quietly reorganized themselves around her fear. She no longer took evening depositions. She routed her walk to the courthouse through longer, more populated streets, adding twenty minutes to her commute each way. She had stopped attending the firm's Friday evening gatherings, offering her husband only vague explanations. He had noticed - he is a patient man, but he had begun to ask questions she did not know how to answer. At night, she lay beside him and could not feel safe in the darkness in the way she once had; she listened to the house, to the street outside, to sounds she had never registered before. If he was late returning from an errand, even by fifteen minutes, she was already composing the worst version of events before she reached for her phone.

It was her husband who finally named what he was watching. He sat with her one evening and said, quietly, that she had not laughed in a very long time. She did not argue. What brought her to the clinic was not a single crisis but an accumulation - the slow recognition that she was living inside a permanent state of alertness that she could not will herself out of, and that it was costing her something she could not afford to keep losing. What she hopes for, she said in the intake session, is to be able to walk into her own courthouse without bracing herself. What she fears is that she no longer knows how.
